questions.question: Explain how unequal heating of the earth builds the global circulation, and apply the model to Africa: the ITCZ's migration, the highs that box in southern Africa, and why the country's two coasts differ.
questions.expected_answer: The sphere is heated unequally: vertical rays concentrate energy at the tropics after a short passage through the atmosphere, while shallow-angle polar rays spread thin after a long slanting journey — giving a surplus equatorward of about 40 degrees and a deficit beyond. Circulation exports the surplus: warm air rises leaving equatorial low pressure, subsides near 30 degrees as the subtropical highs, with subpolar lows near 60 and polar highs over the ice; wind drains from high to low, the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells organise the flow, and Coriolis bends every wind left in the southern hemisphere — turning the returning surface flow into south-east trades and the mid-latitude flow into south-westerlies. The belts migrate a few degrees with the overhead sun. Applied to Africa: the continent straddles the equator, so the master switch is convergence against subsidence. The ITCZ — the thundery seam where the two hemispheres' trades collide — sweeps south with the summer sun to deliver southern Africa's wet season and retreats north in winter, giving the equator two rain seasons and the tropical margins one. Southern Africa is boxed by the South Atlantic High, the South Indian High and winter's Kalahari High, whose subsiding air locks the plateau into dry, frosty, cloudless weather while the displaced westerlies drag fronts across the Cape. The east coast is fed warm moist air across the warm Agulhas current; the west coast is doubly dried — subsiding air above and the cold Benguela current below, yielding fog but almost no rain, the Namib's recipe.

questions.question: Distinguish drought from desertification, grading drought into its four types, and explain how the three arrangements of rock — horizontal, inclined and massive — each produce their own family of landforms.
questions.expected_answer: Drought is rainfall significantly below what a region expects — temporary, and possible even in wet regions — graded as meteorological (the shortfall itself), hydrological (rivers, dams and aquifers drawing down), agricultural (soil moisture failing crops) and socio-economic (livelihoods and food prices affected); El Niño commonly tilts southern African summers toward failure, La Niña toward surplus. Desertification is different: long-term degradation of dryland until it behaves like desert, driven mostly by human causes — overgrazing, overcultivation, fuelwood cutting and salting irrigation — which drought then exposes; examples run from the Sahel to parts of the Karoo and Northern Cape, and management matches each cause: carrying capacity, rotation, drought-hardy planting like the Great Green Wall, contour cultivation and support for the rural poor. Rock arrangements: flat strata under a resistant dolerite cap erode differentially into the tabletop family — plateau to mesa (top wider than height) to butte (height exceeding the narrow top) to conical hill once the cap is stripped. Inclined strata form asymmetrical ridges with a gentle dip slope and steep scarp slope: a cuesta at gentle dip up to about 25 degrees, a homoclinal ridge at moderate dip, and a hogsback where near-vertical strata make both faces steep and matched — the steeper the tilt, the more equal the slopes. Massive granite, unlayered, is exposed as batholith domes that exfoliate in curved onion-skin shells, staying rounded, while jointed blocks rotted underground emerge as stacked tors — Paarl's domes and the Magaliesberg and Matobo castle rocks.

questions.question: Describe the four slope elements and classify mass movements by speed and water content with their priming factors, then explain how these landforms and slopes are read and calculated on a contour map.
questions.expected_answer: Downhill in order: the crest, a convex summit surface rounded by weathering; the cliff or free face, bare bedrock supplying all falling debris; the talus slope, a straight apron of angular rubble at the steepest angle loose rock can hold; and the pediment, a long gently concave foot slope running to the plain — not all slopes carry all four, and in dry South Africa slopes evolve by parallel retreat, the cliff eating back at constant angle while the pediment widens, shrinking mesa to butte to cone. Mass movement is downslope transfer under gravity alone: soil creep, dry and imperceptibly slow, betrayed by leaning fence posts and curved trunks; earthflows and mudflows, wet and fast, with saturated fluid mud the deadliest — as the Merriespruit tailings failure showed; landslides shearing along straight planes and slumps rotating backward along curved ones, leaving crescent scars; and rockfall, blocks dropping free to feed the talus. Priming factors: steepness, water adding weight and lubricating failure planes, undercutting of the slope foot by rivers or road cuts, stripped vegetation, and shaking. On the map: a mesa is a tight ring of crowded contours around an empty top with a widening pediment skirt; a butte the same signature drawn small; a cuesta shows asymmetry — packed on the scarp, spread down the dip; a granite dome draws smooth concentric rings. Gradient is vertical interval over horizontal equivalent stated as one in so many — one hundred metres over two thousand metres is one in twenty; cross-sections are traced crossing by crossing; and intervisibility asks whether a convex bulge humps between the stations and cuts the sight line.
